Testing with one specific vendor driver and hardware is not going to provide additional code coverage beyond what we already have with the in-tree test driver. For simulating ""real"" vendor hardware we plan to add ""profiles"" to the out-of-tree example driver which then more faithfully emulate the number of devices and their attributes of specific hardware.

That leaves integration-style testing *of the vendor's software stack* as justification. Isn't that something that a vendor should be doing? We intentionally publish alpha and release candidates and have a long code freeze period. Vendors can and should use that to make sure that the upcoming Kubernetes release works for them (regarding new features) and doesn't regress. Picking one vendor and doing that work for them won't scale.

column1: I agree that this should ultimately be addressed by a gang-of-gangs abstraction
column2: but I am concerned that an initial implementation may not fully meet the requirements. A natural first approach to gang-of-gangs is to treat each component (e.g.
column3: prefill-leader

column5: decode-leader
column6: decode-worker) as contributing to a single top-level gang with a set of aggregate minCount constraints (for example
column7: at least one prefill leader and one group of three prefill workers)
column8: while still maintaining the existing per-component minCount semantics (e.g.

column1: While this model is sufficient for initial placement
column2: it becomes limiting once scaling is introduced. In particular
column3: it does not provide a clear way to express which components must be gang-scheduled together versus which can scale independently. For example
column4: when scaling both prefill and decode
column5: we typically want prefill leaders and prefill workers to be scheduled as a unit
column6: without being blocked by an inability to schedule additional decode leaders. A flat top-level gang constraint risks coupling unrelated components during scaling

column1: Aside: The difficulties of concisely and clearly encoding these types of constraints while retaining familiar k8s workflows like scaling and rolling updates into resources like Deployment or LeaderWorkerSet are why we built Grove
column2: but Grove is fundamentally still an intent-layer. To be able to provide the full functionality using default kube-scheduler it would need Workload API to support richer semantics around gang-scheduling and eventually topology aware scheduling."

kubernetes/kubernetes;135412;3677034178;aaron-prindle;2025-12-19T23:52:49Z;"@soltysh - RE: the delta from the issue expectation vs. the changes in the PR.  The goal for Declarative Validation is to migrate all supported hand-written code to use declarative validation (for supported validations).  Initially this Umbrella tracking issue was created - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134280 which tracked ""wiring up all the k8s API types for DV"". In talking to API reviewers it was expressed that a PR that wires DV must also migrate at least one DV tag to avoid unused plumbing logic.  This is related to the goal of any DV migration which is to make it possible to rip out the associated hand-written validation code after we let the change soak and confirm our metrics state the errors match identically.  I created https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135752 to help the community find simple DV migration targets to help aid in the PR process for plumbing + adding a tag migration. Notably the fields chosen in this PR aren't actually in  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135752  BUT we still want to migrate supported validations to DV.

Currently the issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/134280 states the below which is actually incorrect from recent discussions (@yongruilin is OOO and the issue description can't be updated atm) as all such DV PRs SHOULD migrate 1+ validations rules:
> Important: Pull requests for this initiative should only enable the declarative validation framework. The migration of existing validation rules will be handled in separate
column2: subsequent PRs.

column1: >- This causes false negatives when quota usage takes longer to reflect the expected size.

kubernetes/kubernetes;134487;3387098243;liggitt;2025-10-09T18:40:48Z;"Some of the CSR and certificates resulting in CI failures contain sloppy subjectAltNames
* emailAddress containing non-email values (unit test only)
* self-signed CA root possibly containing an empty string DNS SAN
* kube-apiserver service serving cert possibly containing an empty DNS name or a name with a trailing dot
* bootstrap client cert containing an empty string DNS name:

Go 1.24.8 and 1.25.2 refuse to parse certificates containing these subjectAltNames. It's unclear whether that tightening was intentional or a side-effect of the rewrite to make cert parsing cheaper and less subject to DOS - xref https://github.com/golang/go/issues/75828#issuecomment-3387061714
While we can (and *should*) improve the correctness of certificates we _produce_ in tests and cluster creation
column2: we *cannot* rebuild with a Go version and release Kubernetes binaries that will instantly break clusters when run with previously issued / accepted / working certificates."

kubernetes/kubernetes;134147;3617586869;danwinship;2025-12-05T16:26:22Z;"/rename Kube-proxy(IPVS): forced resync period changed from 30s to 1h in 1.34

column2: after some debugging with @smoshiur1237
column3: the problem they ran into is just that in 1.33
column4: IPVS kube-proxy ran `syncProxyRules()` every `--ipvs-sync-period` (30s by default) even if no Services or endpoints changed
column5: but with the rewrite of BoundedFrequencyRunner in 1.34 (#131615)
column6: it now only runs `syncProxyRules()` every `proxyutil.FullSyncPeriod` (1h) if no Services or endpoints changed.

column1: Apparently they are doing a test by manually adding ""bad"" ipvs entries with `ipvsadm` and then checking that the bad entries get removed. With 1.33 they would get removed within 30 seconds
column2: but with 1.34 they don't.

column1: My first thought is ""don't do that then""
column2: but OTOH
column3: we don't provide any way to override the BFR `maxInterval`
column4: and this _is_ a change from 1.33 for ipvs and winkernel (though not for iptables or nftables
column5: which already had a hardcoded 1h interval). So I guess we could just revert back from `proxyutil.FullSyncPeriod` to `syncPeriod` for ipvs and winkernel."

I did some testing using the approach of mounting the cgroup path within a privileged pod. I've observed that the container runtime (most probably) is resetting the `memory.high` value inside `/sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice` to the max.

column2: which successfully generated the memory pressure PSI metrics:

column1: sleep 10; i=0; while true; do find /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice -type f -name \""memory.high\"" -exec sh -c 'echo \""195103808\"" | tee {} > /dev/null' \\;; dd if=/dev/zero of=testfile.$i bs=1M count=50 &>/dev/null; i=$(((i+1)%9)); sleep 0.1; done""

column1: django/django;18450;2308643504;charettes;2024-08-25T03:55:35Z;"Thanks for the ping and sorry for the late answer. I'll try to summarize all the points brought so far to
1. Managing to preserve `pk is None` behavior would reduce backward compatibility concerns at the cost of possibly unintuitive magic (if any member of the composition are `None`)
2. Should we have a public of private `_?is_pk_set` method (assuming we can agree on a name) instead

While I think that we should strive to reduce the backward compatibility burden imposed by the introduction of composite primary keys I don't think that focusing on making `pk` return `None` in this case is worthy for two reasons.
The first one being that one way or the other third-party app that ought to support composite primary keys will have to be adapted to expect `pk` to return a `tuple` under some conditions
column2: in this sense `pk is None` is just one pattern that will require adjustments.

column1: The second one is that `pk is None` has always been an _implicit_ way through convention to get an idea of how to treat a `Model` instance. A pattern
column2: just like checking for `_state.adding`
column3: that has been replicated as a symptom of a lack of a blessed way to identify the persistence state of a `Model` instance. In this sense I think that we should see the introduction of composite primary keys as an opportunity to direct the ecosystem towards a blessed way of doing things instead of encouraging this convention further.

The approach I would favor here is to start with a `_is_pk_set` API merged into `main` to validate its merit through documentation but mention it is likely to be superseded eventually through a deprecation period. If we're able to come up with a solution that supersedes both `pk is None` and `_state.adding` checks in a nice way before its release in a distinct work stream it won't be an issue otherwise we'll get to learn through before committing to a solution."

column1: The issue comes when a request body is sent slowly. Previously

column1: > // same as using a multiline string

It should very much _not_ be the same as using a multiline string. The whole point of tagged templates - literally the only reason they are in the language - is that unlike strings they allow using a representation which is immune to problems like sql injection. From your implementation it looks like you're correctly avoiding sql injections
column2: but this is something which should be emphasized in the docs and tested extensively. Users need to be aware that omitting the tag is _not safe_; it's not just a convenience for getting syntax highlighting.

you should also be doing parsing of the string up front: users should get an error as soon as they write ``sql`invalid`;`` rather than needing to actually pass it somewhere to get an error. Note that the first argument to the template tag is always the same value on subsequent calls so that it can be used as a key in a cache instead of needing to check every time the function is called. Probably the easiest thing is to [prepare](https://nodejs.org/api/sqlite.html#databasepreparesql) the statement right away

In Rails 6.x and 7.0 the `tmp/development_secret.txt` file took precedence over the `secret_key_base` defined in `config/credentials.yml.enc` as the original intent of this file was for production use. I remember reading comments when this was introduced where people complained about not being able to have seperate environment based credentials
column2: and the rationale was that `tmp/development_secret.txt` would deal with the only built-in case of needing a key to be different
column3: and that developers could segment their keys within `config/credentials.yml.enc` by environment for certain keys if they wanted to.

column1: Rails 7.1 has a bug or feature that reverses this concept so that if there's a `secret_key_base` in `config/credentials.yml.enc` it always takes precedence over `tmp/local_secret.txt` (as it was renamed). This of course breaks things.
Rails 7.2 and 8.0 (before this PR) reverted the behaviour back to what was experienced in 6.x and 7.0.

I think perhaps users who started out with Rails 7.1 have had their expectations broken with 7.2 and 8.0 but those of us who have been using Rails much longer have also had our expectations broken by 7.1
column2: and soon to be 7.2 and 8.0 via this PR.
